metric_rationale: Focuses specifically on the critical trial where Option A has more positive features (favored by Tallying) but Option B has the highest validity features (favored by WADD). The metric calculates the proportion of times the high-validity option (Option B in Trial 1) is chosen. Tallying predicts a value near 0, whereas WADD predicts a value near 1.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices consistent with the Weighted Additive (WADD) model on the critical trials where WADD and Tallying strongly disagree. In these trials, one option has fewer positive features but those features have much higher validity (e.g., A=[1,1,0,0,0] vs B=[0,0,1,1,1]). Tallying simply counts wins and prefers the option with 3 positive features, whereas WADD weights by validity and generally prefers the option with the 2 highly valid features. A value close to 1 supports WADD, while a value close to 0 supports Tallying.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. The experimental design specifically includes 'critical trials' where the single most valid discriminating feature points to one option, while the sum of all other less valid features points to the other option. On these trials, TTB and WADD will make completely opposite predictions. Therefore, data generated by the TTB model will yield a high score on this metric (close to 1.0, modulo noise), whereas data generated by the WADD model will yield a very low score (close to 0.0, or random chance depending on noise), creating a massive, robust mean gap and low per-subject variance.

In this specific experimental design, the Compensatory WADD model will consistently favor the option with the higher total number of positive features (equivalent to the Tallying choice) because the sum of the less valid features outweighs the single most valid feature in the critical trials. Conversely, the non-compensatory Take The Best (TTB) model relies entirely on the first discriminating feature, which in 6 out of the 7 trials favors the option with the *fewer* total positive features. By calculating the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option with the greater sum of positive features, we perfectly capture the opposing predictions of the two models: WADD will score very high (close to 1.0, minus noise), whereas TTB will score very low (around 1/7, plus noise).

Under Random Guessing, the probability of choosing option B is 0.5 across all trial types, so the variance of the mean responses across the 10 unique trial types will be small (only reflecting binomial noise). Under the Weighted Additive (WADD) model, choice probabilities systematically vary from near 0 (when A is strongly preferred) to near 1 (when B is strongly preferred), resulting in a much larger variance of mean responses across trial types.

Calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the option that has the higher objective weighted sum (using the provided validities). For Random Guessing, this proportion will be consistently near 0.5. For the WADD model, choices will align with the higher weighted sum on average, resulting in a proportion significantly greater than 0.5.

This metric computes the proportion of trials where the subject chose the option with the strictly greater number of positive features (excluding ties). Under the Random Guessing theory, subjects ignore features entirely, so this proportion will be tightly centered around 0.5. Under the Random Feature Heuristic, subjects sample a feature and choose the option with a higher value on that feature, which statistically favors the option with more positive features overall, leading to a proportion significantly greater than 0.5. The exclusion of tie trials maximizes the expected contrast.

The Random Feature Heuristic predicts that the probability of choosing Option A increases as the difference in the number of positive features between A and B increases. Random Guessing predicts a flat 50% probability regardless of the features. This metric computes the mean rate of choosing A when A has more positive features than B, minus the mean rate of choosing A when A has fewer positive features. For Random Guessing, this difference will be approximately 0. For the Random Feature Heuristic, it will be significantly positive.

Under the Random Guessing theory, each subject chooses Option A with exactly 50% probability on every trial, so their overall choice proportion will be very close to 0.5 (with only small binomial variance). Under the Spatial Bias theory, subjects have an idiosyncratic baseline preference between 0.3 and 0.7, meaning their choice proportions will systematically deviate from 0.5. By calculating the squared deviation of each subject's choice proportion from 0.5 and averaging this across subjects, we obtain a metric that is near zero for Random Guessing but substantially higher for Spatial Bias. Computing this at the subject level before averaging ensures the metric correctly captures the between-subject variance in bias.

Spatial Bias predicts that subjects have an idiosyncratic preference for one option over the other, meaning their overall choice proportions will deviate significantly from 0.5 (reflecting their individual bias). Random Guessing predicts choice proportions will be tightly clustered around 0.5, as choices are essentially coin flips. By calculating the squared deviation of each subject's choice proportion from 0.5, we can clearly distinguish the wider distribution of Spatial Bias from the narrow distribution of Random Guessing.
